profile.summary: SpliceTransformer (SpTransformer) predicts RNA splicing from genomic sequence alone. For each position in a pre-mRNA sequence it gives the probability of being a splice donor, a splice acceptor or neither, and how much the site is used in each of 15 human tissues. Comparing predictions for reference and variant sequence lets it score how a genetic variant changes splicing in each tissue.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Results, Tissue-specific prediction of splicing; Fig. 1 caption. README: title paragraph

summary_quotes.text: The SpliceTransformer (SpTransformer) is a deep learning tool designed to predict tissue-specific splicing sites from pre-mRNA sequences.

SpTransformer is a computational model that predicts the probability of each position in a pre-mRNA input sequence being a splice donor, splice acceptor, or neither in all and 15 different tissues simultaneously

The SpTransformer model takes an only sequence as input and predicts tissue-specific splicing in 15 human tissues. The model can be used to evaluate genetic variants and predict tissue-specific splicing alterations.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: SpTransformer has two main modules. An encoder of stacked convolutional residual blocks (ResBlocks) reads one-hot encoded sequence; the paper uses two such encoders with identical structure. Their output feeds a Sinkhorn Transformer, an attention variant built for long sequences, with 256 channels, 8 attention heads (two of them local) per layer and eight layers, followed by a multi-layer perceptron. For a 9000 nt input it predicts the central 1000 nt, using 4000 nt of context on each side. The output is an N x 3 matrix for splice site class and an N x 15 matrix for tissue usage. Training ran in two stages: first the two encoders were trained separately, one on GTEx data and one on an extra mammalian dataset, with 12 epochs per stage.

quotes.text: SpTransformer is a large deep neural network model that consists of two main modules: an encoder module and a transformer module.
The encoder module incorporates a series of residual networks, known as ResBlock
The second component of our model mainly consists of a Sinkhorn Transformer module and a multi-layer perception module.
The Sinkhorn Transformer module has 256 channels, 8 attention heads (including two local attention heads) per layer, and eight layers of depth.

Specifically, for an RNA sequence of length 9000 nt, SpTransformer utilized the sequence context to predict splicing sites and their corresponding usage in 15 tissues for the central 1000 nt sequence.
representing splice site prediction and tissue usage prediction, respectively.

two stages of training. In the first stage, two convolution-based encoder modules with identical structures were trained separately. One module learned weights from the GTEx training dataset, while the other module learned weights from the excessive training dataset
The model was trained for 12 epochs in each stage.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The repository describes one trained model. Its weights are too large for GitHub; Git-LFS access was disabled in November 2024, and the weights are now a single Google Drive download placed in model/weights. The download has no version label, so a result can only name the repository commit (this page read b67a51da) and the date the weights were fetched. The authors note that outputs can differ slightly between GPU types for individual variants. The variant annotation script uses a 95% threshold for tissue specificity unless raw scores are requested, so a result should say which output mode was used.

strengths.text: Predicts splice site usage for 15 human tissues at once from sequence alone, with no RNA-seq input needed at prediction time.

quotes.text: The SpTransformer model takes an only sequence as input and predicts tissue-specific splicing in 15 human tissues.

strengths.text: Ships a ready variant annotation command that takes a VCF and writes a prediction table, with an example input in the repository and a CPU option for small inputs.

quotes.text: python sptransformer.py --input data/example/input38.vcf --output data/example/output38.tsv --reference hg38
the lightweight example data can also be handled with CPU only

strengths.text: Training adds RNA-seq splicing data from three non-human mammals; the authors report that their ablation shows this improves both splice site and tissue usage prediction.

quotes.text: These observations underscore that the inclusion of an extra mammalian dataset enhances both the identification of splice sites and the tissue-specificity prediction.

run_guide.summary: Clone the repository, build the conda environment, add the weights and reference files, and annotate the example VCF with tissue-specific splicing predictions.
prerequisites: Linux (tested on CentOS 7 and Red Hat 4.8.5). A GPU is recommended; the example data also runs on CPU.
conda, with Python 3.8 and PyTorch 1.10 as in the README example.
The weights file from Google Drive, the hg38 genome FASTA and a GENCODE annotation file.
Code is Apache-2.0. No separate licence is stated for the weights.
